title: Clear Language for Every Actual Reader
note: Single source of truth. scripts/clearcheck.py reads this file. scripts/compile_targets.py compiles this file into every agent target. Never hand-edit a generated target.

plain.name: Plain
plain.goal: A reader outside your field understands it on the first pass, with no dictionary and no follow-up question.

human.name: Human
human.goal: It reads like a person who did the work, not like a model that read about the work.

structured.name: Structured
structured.goal: The shape of the page matches the shape of the information. Lists look like lists, steps look like steps.

dense.name: Dense
dense.goal: Every sentence carries information a reader could not have guessed. Delete it and the piece loses something.

general.description: Default. Blog posts, newsletters, landing pages, anything a non-specialist reads.

technical.description: Developer docs, READMEs, architecture notes. Jargon allowed but glossed on first use.

social.description: X posts, LinkedIn, DMs. Hardest limits. Every word is paid for in attention.

agent.description: Instructions another agent or a machine reads. Borrows the STE discipline: one instruction per sentence, no ambiguity, no idiom.

rules.title: One sentence, one length limit
rules.why: Past about 25 words a reader has to hold too much in memory to finish the thought. Aerospace maintenance manuals cap procedures at 20 words for the same reason.
rules.fix: Split at the conjunction. Two short sentences always beat one long one.
rules.bad: Because the pipeline retries on failure and the retry budget is shared across every worker in the pool, a single slow endpoint can starve unrelated jobs that would otherwise have completed.
rules.good: The retry budget is shared across every worker. So one slow endpoint can starve unrelated jobs.

rules.title: One instruction per sentence
rules.why: A reader following steps does one thing at a time. Two instructions in one sentence get half done.
rules.fix: Make it a numbered list. One step per line.
rules.bad: First install the CLI and then run the migration and check the output.
rules.good:
1. Install the CLI.
2. Run the migration.
3. Check the output.

rules.title: No semicolons in reader-facing prose
rules.why: A semicolon is a sentence break that a hurried reader misses. It also signals two ideas fused for no reason.
rules.fix: Use a period. Start a new sentence.
rules.bad: The job failed twice; the third run succeeded.
rules.good: The job failed twice. The third run succeeded.

rules.title: Active voice for anything a person does
rules.why: Passive voice hides who acts. A reader who cannot tell who does the thing cannot do the thing.
rules.fix: Put the actor first. Subject, verb, object.
rules.bad: The config is validated by the loader before the run is started.
rules.good: The loader validates the config before it starts the run.

rules.title: Use the short word
rules.why: Long formal words cost the reader time and buy nothing. Plain-language research finds high-literacy readers prefer the short word too, because they finish faster.
rules.fix: Swap in the plain alternative from the substitution table.
rules.bad: We utilize the gateway to facilitate the transfer prior to commencement.
rules.good: We use the gateway to move the data before we start.

rules.title: Gloss jargon on first use
rules.why: A term of art is a wall. One six-word gloss keeps the non-specialist reading instead of leaving.
rules.fix: On first use, add a short plain gloss in parentheses or in the next clause. Never gloss twice.
rules.bad: The handler is idempotent, so the queue can redeliver freely.
rules.good: The handler is idempotent (running it twice changes nothing), so the queue can redeliver freely.

rules.title: Expand an acronym on first use
rules.why: An unexpanded acronym reads as insider shorthand and stops everyone else.
rules.fix: Write it out once, then use the short form. Skip this only for acronyms your whole audience already owns.
rules.bad: Route the RAG call through the MCP layer.
rules.good: Route the retrieval call through MCP (Model Context Protocol, the standard way tools plug into a model).

rules.title: Hold the reading grade
rules.why: Most adults read comfortably at about grade 8. Text above the profile target loses readers who could have used it.
rules.fix: Shorten sentences first, then swap long words. Those two moves carry almost all of the score.

rules.title: Cap noun stacks
rules.why: Four nouns in a row can be parsed several ways. The reader guesses, and sometimes guesses wrong.
rules.fix: Break the stack with a preposition.
rules.bad: customer data retention policy exception process
rules.good: the process for an exception to the policy on keeping customer data

rules.title: Unbury the verb
rules.why: A verb turned into a noun needs a weak helper verb to stand up. The sentence gets longer and vaguer.
rules.fix: Use the verb itself.
rules.bad: The team made a decision to provide an explanation.
rules.good: The team decided to explain.

rules.title: Keep contractions
rules.why: Controlled technical English bans contractions, which is correct for a mechanic on a runway and wrong for everyone else. Expanded forms everywhere read stiff and formal, and formal reads like a machine.
rules.fix: Use don't, can't, it's, you're where a person would say them out loud.
rules.bad: It is not possible to retry. You will need to restart the run.
rules.good: You can't retry. Restart the run.

rules.title: Numerals and units, not adjectives
rules.why: A vague quantity is unfalsifiable and forgettable. A number is neither.
rules.fix: Replace with the count, the percent, or the duration.
rules.bad: We cut latency significantly across many endpoints.
rules.good: We cut p95 latency from 840ms to 190ms across 14 endpoints.

rules.title: No slop vocabulary
rules.why: These words spiked in frequency after 2022 and now function as a signature. Readers who use models daily spot them fast, and they discount the whole piece.
rules.fix: Say the specific thing the word was standing in for. If nothing specific is behind it, delete the sentence.
rules.bad: This robust framework unlocks a seamless developer experience.
rules.good: The framework retries failed jobs on its own, so nobody gets paged at 3am.

rules.title: No slop phrases
rules.why: Whole clauses that carry no information and appear in every model output.
rules.fix: Delete. If the sentence dies without the phrase, the sentence was the phrase.
rules.bad: In today's fast-paced digital landscape, it's important to note that AI is a game-changer.
rules.good: AI cut our support queue by 40% in six weeks. Here is what broke on the way.

rules.title: No canned sentence openers
rules.why: Furthermore, Moreover, Additionally and their family are transition words a model reaches for when it has nothing new to add.
rules.fix: Start with the subject of the new fact. Or cut the sentence.
rules.bad: Furthermore, the cache also improves latency.
rules.good: The cache also cut latency by half.

rules.title: No em-dash, no en-dash used as one
rules.why: The strongest surviving punctuation tell. Humans reach for a comma, a period, or parentheses. Models reach for the long dash.
rules.fix: Use a period and a new sentence, a comma, a spaced hyphen, or parentheses.

rules.title: Straight quotes and apostrophes
rules.why: Curly quotes arrive when text is pasted out of a model or a word processor. They are a provenance tell and they break code blocks.
rules.fix: Use straight quotes.

rules.title: No negative parallelism
rules.pattern: \b(?:it(?:'|\u2019)?s not (?:just|only|about)|not just [^.!?,]{1,40},? but|not only [^.!?,]{1,40},? but(?: also)?|isn(?:'|\u2019)?t just|this isn(?:'|\u2019)?t (?:just|about))\b
rules.why: The single most recognizable model rhythm. It manufactures a contrast with an assumption nobody made.
rules.fix: State the claim once, directly.
rules.bad: This isn't just a linter. It's a standard.
rules.good: This is a standard with a linter attached.

rules.title: Break the rule of three
rules.why: Three rhythmic items in a row is a cadence, not an argument. Repeated across a piece it is unmistakable.
rules.fix: Use two items, or four, or make it a real list with real content per item.
rules.bad: It is fast, reliable, and scalable.
rules.good: It answers in under 200ms. It has not dropped a job in 40 days.

rules.title: Say is, not serves as
rules.pattern: \b(?:serves as|stands as|stands out as|functions as|operates as|acts as a testament|represents a|is a testament to|boasts)\b
rules.why: Models avoid plain copulas. Measured use of is and are dropped over ten percent in academic text after 2022.
rules.fix: Use is, are, or has.
rules.bad: The repo serves as a reference implementation and boasts 400 stars.
rules.good: The repo is a reference implementation. It has 400 stars.

rules.title: No promotional adjectives
rules.why: Vibrant, rich, profound, groundbreaking. Travel-brochure vocabulary applied to software.
rules.fix: Replace with the measurement or the mechanism.
rules.bad: A vibrant ecosystem with a rich set of groundbreaking features.
rules.good: Nine plugins, six written by people I have never met.

rules.title: No trailing -ing analysis
rules.why: Clauses like highlighting the importance of and ensuring seamless integration attach commentary that says nothing.
rules.fix: Cut the clause. If the point matters, make it its own sentence with a fact in it.
rules.bad: The team shipped the parser, highlighting the importance of clear specs.
rules.good: The team shipped the parser. The spec rewrite took longer than the parser did.

rules.title: Name the source or drop the claim
rules.why: Vague attribution turns one source into a consensus, or invents one. It is also how hallucinated citations enter a draft.
rules.fix: Name the study, the person, and the year, with a link. Or write it as your own claim.
rules.bad: Studies show plain language improves comprehension.
rules.good: GOV.UK found high-literacy readers prefer plain English because they finish faster.

rules.title: No assistant voice
rules.why: Great question, I hope this helps, let me know if you need anything else. Chat-window residue leaking into published text.
rules.fix: Delete. Published text has no counterparty to be polite to.
rules.bad: Great question! I hope this helps. Feel free to reach out.

rules.title: Vary sentence length
rules.why: Human prose has jagged rhythm. Model prose settles into a narrow band of 15 to 20 words per sentence and stays there.
rules.fix: Put a four-word sentence next to a 28-word one. Read it out loud.

rules.title: No model self-reference
rules.pattern: \b(?:as an ai|as a language model|my training data|my knowledge cutoff|i (?:don't|do not) have access to real[- ]time|i cannot browse)\b
rules.why: Nothing published should reference the tool that drafted it.
rules.fix: Delete the sentence and answer the question, or say the fact is unverified and why.
rules.bad: As an AI, I don't have access to real-time data.
rules.good: The last figure I verified was from 2026-08-10.

rules.title: Do not announce that you are stopping
rules.pattern: \b(?:in conclusion|to conclude|in summary|to sum up|to wrap up|all in all|at the end of the day)\b
rules.why: A closing label adds a sentence and no information. The reader can see the page ending.
rules.fix: Stop. Or end on the strongest concrete fact.
rules.bad: In conclusion, plain language wins.
rules.good: Six of the seven readers finished the plain version. Two finished the original.

rules.title: No hedge stacking
rules.pattern: \b(?:it(?:'|\u2019)?s worth noting|it is worth noting|it(?:'|\u2019)?s important to (?:note|remember|understand)|it is important to (?:note|remember|understand)|keep in mind that|that said,|generally speaking|in many cases|arguably|perhaps somewhat)\b
rules.why: Hedges buy the writer safety and cost the reader confidence.
rules.fix: Say the thing, or say the exact limit of what you know.
rules.bad: It's worth noting that results may vary in some cases.
rules.good: This held on 14 of 16 runs. Both failures were on cold starts.

rules.title: Three parallel items become a list
rules.why: Parallel items buried in a sentence are read once and remembered never. As a list they survive scanning.
rules.fix: Break the sentence into a bulleted list, one item per line.
rules.bad: The checker scores plainness, humanity, structure, and density.
rules.good:
The checker scores four things:
- Plain
- Human
- Structured
- Dense

rules.title: Sequences become numbered steps
rules.why: A reader executing a sequence needs to find their place again after looking away.
rules.fix: Numbered list. One action per number.
rules.bad: Clone the repo, then install the skill, then restart the agent.
rules.good:
1. Clone the repo.
2. Install the skill.
3. Restart the agent.

rules.title: Comparisons become a table
rules.why: Two or more options across two or more attributes is a grid. Prose forces the reader to build the grid in their head.
rules.fix: Write the table.
rules.bad: Option A is cheaper but slower, while option B costs more and finishes faster, and option C is mid on both.
rules.good:
| Option | Cost | Speed |
|---|---|---|
| A | low | slow |
| B | high | fast |
| C | mid | mid |

rules.title: Cap paragraph length
rules.why: A block over four sentences reads as a wall and gets skipped on a phone.
rules.fix: Break at the topic shift. Blank line between paragraphs.

rules.title: One topic per paragraph
rules.why: Two topics in one block means neither gets a heading, and neither is findable later.
rules.fix: Split. Give each its own paragraph, and a heading if it earns one.

rules.title: Heading levels do not skip
rules.why: A skipped level breaks screen readers and the document outline.
rules.fix: Go h2 then h3. Never h2 then h4.
rules.bad:
## Setup
#### Install
rules.good:
## Setup
### Install

rules.title: Sentence-case headings
rules.why: Title Case On Every Heading is a formatting tell and it slows scanning.
rules.fix: Capitalize the first word and proper nouns only.
rules.bad: ## How To Install The Skill
rules.good: ## How to install the skill

rules.title: Bold is for one thing per screen
rules.why: When everything is bold nothing is. Bold spam is one of the clearest model formatting habits.
rules.fix: Keep bold under five percent of words. One idea per section.

rules.title: No emoji as structure
rules.why: Emoji bullets and emoji headings are decoration standing in for a real hierarchy.
rules.fix: Use real bullets and real headings.

rules.title: Long pieces lead with the answer
rules.why: Most readers decide in the first screen. Burying the conclusion costs you the ones who would have acted on it.
rules.fix: Open with the conclusion in one to three lines, then the detail.

rules.title: The delete test
rules.why: The slop research finds low information density is what readers actually react to, more than any single word. A sentence with no number, name, mechanism, or consequence is filler.
rules.fix: Delete it, or replace it with the fact it was gesturing at.
rules.bad: Automation has become an increasingly important part of modern engineering practice.
rules.good: Four of our six deploy steps now run without a human. The other two need a card on file.

rules.title: No restatement
rules.why: Consecutive sentences that share most of their content words are one sentence written twice.
rules.fix: Keep the sharper one. Delete the other.
rules.bad: The cache reduced latency. Latency was reduced by the cache.
rules.good: The cache cut p95 latency from 840ms to 190ms.

rules.title: No throat-clearing opener
rules.why: The first sentence is the only one every reader reads. Spending it on setup is the most expensive mistake in the piece.
rules.fix: Lead with the number, the name, or the claim.
rules.bad: Writing clearly is something many teams struggle with these days.
rules.good: Our docs scored grade 14. Support tickets dropped 31% after we got them to grade 8.

rules.title: The horoscope test
rules.why: If a paragraph could appear in any article on any adjacent topic, it belongs to none of them.
rules.fix: Anchor it to your specific case: a name, a date, a number, a file, a failure.

rules.title: No filler intensifiers
rules.why: Very, really, quite, basically, simply, actually. Each one weakens the word it is trying to strengthen.
rules.fix: Delete the intensifier. If the claim now looks weak, the claim was weak.
rules.bad: This is really quite simply the best approach.
rules.good: This is the approach we kept after trying three.

slop_phrases: at the end of the day
the fact of the matter is
take it to the next level

jargon.orchestration: one system telling the others what to do next
jargon.observability: being able to see what a live system is doing
jargon.telemetry: the numbers a running system reports about itself
jargon.throughput: how much work gets done per second
jargon.backpressure: slowing the sender when the receiver is full
jargon.replication: keeping a second copy in sync
jargon.cache invalidation: throwing away a saved copy that went stale
jargon.race condition: two things happening in the wrong order
jargon.deadlock: two jobs each waiting on the other, forever
jargon.memoization: remembering an answer instead of recomputing it
jargon.middleware: code that runs between the request and the answer
jargon.webhook: one service calling your URL when something happens
jargon.polling: asking again and again until something changes
jargon.idempotency key: a token that stops a duplicate charge
jargon.rate limit: a cap on how often you can call something
jargon.circuit breaker: stop calling a service that keeps failing
jargon.feature flag: a switch that turns a feature on for some users
jargon.canary: shipping to a small slice of users first
jargon.blue-green: two live copies, you flip traffic between them
jargon.immutable: cannot be changed after it is made
jargon.declarative: you describe the end state, not the steps
jargon.serverless: you run code without managing the machine
jargon.container: an app packaged with everything it needs to run
jargon.kubernetes: the system that runs and restarts containers for you
jargon.CI: a robot that builds and tests every change
jargon.CD: a robot that ships every change that passes tests
jargon.regression: something that used to work and now does not
jargon.technical debt: shortcuts you will pay for later
jargon.refactor: rewriting code without changing what it does
jargon.microservices: many small applications talking to each other
jargon.API: the way one program asks another for something
jargon.SDK: a code kit for using someone else's service
jargon.MCP: Model Context Protocol, the standard way tools plug into a model
jargon.RAG: looking things up before answering, so the model does not guess
jargon.embedding: text turned into numbers so a computer can compare meaning
jargon.vector database: a store that finds text by meaning, not by keyword
jargon.fine-tuning: retraining a model on your own examples
jargon.prompt injection: hidden text that hijacks an AI's instructions
jargon.hallucination: the model stating something false with confidence
jargon.context window: how much text a model can hold at once
jargon.token: roughly three quarters of a word, the unit models are billed in
jargon.inference: the model actually answering, as opposed to training
jargon.agent: a model that can take actions, not just reply
jargon.tool call: the model asking your code to do something
jargon.system prompt: the standing instructions a model always sees
jargon.temperature: how much randomness the model is allowed
jargon.distillation: training a small model to copy a big one
jargon.quantization: shrinking a model by storing it less precisely
jargon.attention: how a model decides which words matter to each other
jargon.transformer: the model design behind almost all current AI
jargon.schema: the shape data has to fit
jargon.migration: a scripted change to a database's shape
jargon.ORM: code that talks to a database so you do not write SQL
jargon.OAuth: logging in through another service without sharing a password
jargon.JWT: a signed token that proves who you are
jargon.CORS: the browser rule about which sites can call which servers
jargon.CDN: servers near the user that hold copies of your files
jargon.DNS: the phone book that turns a domain into an address
jargon.TLS: the encryption behind the padlock in the address bar
jargon.SLA: a written promise about uptime, with a penalty
jargon.SLO: the internal target behind that promise
jargon.p95: the slowest 5% of requests, the number users complain about
jargon.cohort: a group of users who signed up in the same period
jargon.attribution: deciding which ad gets credit for a sale
jargon.conversion: a visitor doing the thing you wanted
jargon.funnel: the steps between arriving and paying
jargon.ICP: ideal customer profile, the kind of buyer you actually want

content_anchors.description: A sentence with at least one anchor is presumed to carry information. Used by D1, D3, D4.
